cues.text: An Earthquake Off the Pacific Coast
On the morning of January 31, 1906, at roughly ten-thirty, one of the most powerful earthquakes ever recorded struck off Ecuador and Colombia.
8, its tremors lasted nearly ten minutes and were felt across the region.
On the small Pacific island of Tumaco, in southwestern Colombia, the sea began to retreat nearly a kilometer from shore, the unmistakable warning sign of an approaching tsunami.
A Procession to the Water's Edge
Terrified residents ran to their parish church and begged their pastor, the Augustinian Recollect priest Fray Gerardo Larrondo, to intercede for them.
Larrondo consumed the smaller consecrated Hosts kept in the ciborium, took up the large Host, and called out to his people, "Let us go, my people.
Let us go toward the beach, and may God have pity on us."
The community set out for the shore together, weeping and praying as they went.
A Wave That Turned Back
As a wall of water estimated at up to five meters high rushed toward the town, Father Larrondo reached the water's edge, raised the Host, and traced the sign of the cross over the advancing wave.
According to numerous witnesses, the wave halted its advance, hesitated, and then receded back into the ocean, sparing Tumaco.
Other communities along the same stretch of coast suffered devastating losses, with between five hundred and fifteen hundred people killed by the same tsunami elsewhere.
"Miracle! Miracle!"
The people of Tumaco are said to have cried out together, "Milagro!
Milagro!"
— Miracle!
Miracle!
— as the water withdrew, and the Blessed Sacrament was carried back and solemnly enthroned in the church.
Word of what had happened spread well beyond the island; Father Larrondo reportedly received letters from as far away as Europe asking for his prayers in the years that followed.
Legacy
Tumaco has marked the anniversary of January 31 every year since with processions, Eucharistic adoration, and formal acts of thanksgiving.
In 2026, the Diocese of Tumaco celebrated the tradition's 120th anniversary with forty hours of adoration and a stated hope of building a dedicated shrine at the cathedral.
Among the Eucharistic accounts gathered by St. Carlo Acutis for his exhibition, Tumaco stands out for the plainness of what it asks a visitor to believe.
Not a vision or a transformation, but a wave that, by the testimony of an entire town, simply stopped.
